content.title: About
content.content: Collards (leafy cabbage) are a leafy vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, closely related to kale. They have large, slightly bitter leaves, a nutrient‑dense profile, and are commonly cooked, including sautéed in oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards thrive in temperate climates and can tolerate light frosts.
The deep green color comes from high chlorophyll content.
Unlike spinach, collard leaves retain their texture during long cooking.
In the Southern United States they are traditionally cooked with smoked meat and spices.
Collard seeds can be ground into a mustard‑like powder.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Collards provide a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C support immune function and vision.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collards contain oxalates, which may increase kidney‑stone risk in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Like other cruciferous vegetables, excessive raw consumption can affect thyroid function.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to Brassica vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Collards are typically sautéed in a small amount of oil until tender, added to stews, soups, or salads. Raw leaves can be blended into smoothies, but a quick blanch reduces oxalate levels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store collards in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container with a bit of moisture. They stay fresh for 5‑7 days. For longer storage, blanch and freeze the leaves.
